name: Freya Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I play flute for a small chamber orchestra, record warm-up lines and teach three pupils at the arts centre. I have a bachelor’s degree in music and have been paid to play for twenty-four years. The flute case is light; carrying a patchwork of rehearsal dates in my head is the tiring bit.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does that patchwork mean at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58 and our children are grown. My partner has regular postal shifts, we rent our flat and have four months of expenses saved. I earn about the usual amount for this work, and there are some other groups nearby, though a nearby group is not automatically hiring. I use a paper calendar and have never used AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the orchestra that a faster booking notice is useful if it still shows the musician’s fee and rehearsal time. A screen cannot breathe through my flute phrase.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Four months saved and my partner’s regular wage can carry a late rehearsal payment. I still want every date in writing because last winter’s cancelled concert left a hole in the month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I would confirm the next six paid calls and my three pupil slots, and ask for a written cancellation fee. In the first year of this mild change I would keep playing and teaching, checking any digital notice against my paper calendar rather than learning an AI app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the next few months. One shifted date would be irritating, but our rent would still be covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the cancelled concert cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The organiser paid rehearsal time but not the performance. I marked the gap in red and used savings rather than asking our grown children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you sign up for an AI scheduler?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do not use AI now, and the paper calendar works for me. I would need a clear paid reason before changing it.

say: I would welcome **faster notices** with musician fees and rehearsal times visible.
I would say **live flute playing** still needs a player’s breath.
think: Our **four-month reserve** and partner wage cover one delayed fee.
A **written cancellation term** matters after last winter’s unpaid concert.
do: Confirm **six paid calls** and three pupil slots this week.
Request **written cancellation pay** and check notices against my paper calendar.
feel: I feel **calm** with paid dates, savings and regular household wages.
S0.quote: A screen cannot breathe through my flute phrase.
fieldNote: Her **experienced flute work** earns typical pay with four months saved and some nearby groups.
She has **never used AI** and keeps a paper calendar by choice.

steps.text: Confirm six paid orchestra calls and three pupils this week
Request written cancellation fee and check notices against paper calendar

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the arts centre that generated flute warm-ups might replace recordings it buys from me. I would bring our fee sheets to the musicians’ association so preparation and cancellation pay stay visible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Those recordings bring about a quarter of my own pay. Four months saved buys time, but a permanent cut would still lower what we can put aside for later life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would compare six months of warm-up invoices with the centre’s new orders and take the figures to the association. In the first year, if recording orders fall, I would stop renting my separate practice room on unused days, keep the three paid pupils and orchestra calls, and ask the centre for signed paid dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel anxious about a realistic cut to recording pay. I can bargain from flute invoices, but I cannot make the arts centre order another track.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the association to seek?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We need a minimum recording fee that includes preparation, not a warm statement about valuing artists. The centre can see what each take actually cost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the new recording software?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have never used AI and will not upload a pupil’s playing to find out. I would listen to a trusted colleague explain it, but I am not paying for a trial.

say: I would warn **generated warm-ups** could replace paid recordings.
I would bring **fee sheets** to the musicians’ association for preparation and cancellation pay.
think: Warm-up lines make **one-quarter of my pay**, so a lasting cut matters.
Four **months saved** buy time but not a new regular wage.
do: Compare **warm-up invoices** and bring order figures to the association now.
Stop **unused room hire** after recording cuts; keep paid pupils/orchestra and request signed centre dates.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a plausible loss of my recording fees.
S1.quote: I can bargain from flute invoices, but I cannot make the arts centre order another track.
fieldNote: Her **collective fee request** has a specific rate and preparation cost behind it.
The **room saving** starts only after orders fall, while current paid teaching and orchestra work continue.

steps.text: Compare six months of warm-up invoices and bring figures to musicians association
Stop separate practice-room hire on unused days after recording orders fall
Keep three paid pupils/orchestra calls and request signed centre dates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my pupils that thinking AGI by 2028 could make a flute warm-up track before any robot plays a flute. Playing robots come around 2031, three years later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the warm-up orders to end in 2028, taking about a quarter of my own pay. Live calls could also fall, but four months saved and my partner’s wage give me some time to find actual paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I would total recording invoices, request a signed paid orchestra calendar and ask for an actual pension estimate before thinking about stopping at sixty. In the first year after 2028, if paid live calls fall too, I would seek a posted school music-tutor job only if my degree and teaching experience qualify, written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and the bus works; I would keep orchestra calls and pupils until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about losing a regular quarter of my pay. I would be alarmed if live work collapsed too, but I do not expect that from the bookings I have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the school job open now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check current paid postings and their teaching requirements. A school I once visited is not a vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would savings let you retire at sixty?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Four months saved are useful for a search, not years of rent. I need the actual pension estimate before naming any stopping date.

say: I would distinguish **2028 thinking AGI** from 2031 flute-playing robots.
I would say **warm-up tracks** could be made before playing robots arrive.
think: I expect **one-quarter of my pay** from warm-up orders to end.
Our **four-month reserve** gives a search window if live calls also shrink.
do: Total **recording invoices**, request a signed orchestra calendar and actual pension estimate now.
Seek **posted tutor work** after 2028 live cuts only if degree/teaching qualify, written net after travel replaces losses and bus fits.
Keep **orchestra and pupils** until a suitable signed offer.
feel: I feel **anxious** about my own expected recording loss.
S2.quote: Four months saved are useful for a search, not years of rent.
fieldNote: The **expected 2028 track loss** precedes 2031 flute-playing robots; live cuts remain conditional.
A **tutor move** needs a current qualified posting, replacement net pay after travel, bus access and signed offer.

steps.text: Total recording invoices; request signed orchestra calendar and actual pension estimate now
Seek posted tutor job after live cuts if music degree/teaching qualify and bus fits
Require written net after travel replacing losses; keep paid music until signed offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the centre that five years to AGI by 2031 lets us price a paid flute beginners’ circle properly. Flute-playing robots follow around 2034, so I would want a real room agreement first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Recording orders may dry up before 2031, but I know how to teach breath and fingering. A class only helps if it pays for my preparation as well as the chairs and the journey.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next spring I would get written hall and hire terms showing insurance coverage and charges before taking deposits, then fit a separate four-week flute circle around booked orchestra calls. I would run it only if five adults prepay enough for room, insurance, cleaning, my teaching, preparation and bus travel, with inspected centre loan flutes provided without a separate hire fee or sound instruments they own. In the first year after 2031 I would repeat only while those written insured room terms hold and five paid safe places cover the same costs; if too few adults pay or an unsafe flute leaves fewer than five, I would restore five safe paid places or defer and refund everyone, keeping my three pupils and booked orchestra calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious until five fees clear. My flute class cannot pay its own way with four safe places.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who checks a loan flute?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The centre instrument keeper must check keys, pads and cleaning before anyone plays. An unsafe flute cannot be counted as a paid safe place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if four adults prepay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would refund all four instead of borrowing from our reserve for hall rent. My three existing pupils already have paid lessons booked.

say: I would propose a **paid flute beginners’ circle** at the centre.
I would require a **real room agreement** before announcing places.
think: Five **paid safe places** must cover insured room hire, cleaning, my teaching/preparation and bus travel.
do: Start **flute circle** outside paid calls after written insured hire; require five fees covering room/insurance, cleaning, teaching/preparation, travel and safe flutes.
Renew **circle after 2031** only with written insured room and five paid safe places covering hire/insurance, cleaning, teaching/preparation and travel.
Replace **unsafe flutes** or defer/refund everyone below five safe paid places from missing buyers or safety; keep booked calls/pupils.
feel: I feel **anxious** until the separate class pays its costs.
S3.quote: My flute class cannot pay its own way with four safe places.
fieldNote: The **five-place floor** pays insured written room hire, teaching/preparation, cleaning and travel; inspected centre loan flutes carry no separate hire fee.
A **short enrollment** or failed safety check triggers replacement or whole-group refund; class hours avoid booked paid calls.

steps.text: Secure written insured hire; schedule around booked calls before five fees cover room/insurance, cleaning, teaching/prep, travel
Inspect loan flutes; replace unsafe places or refund everyone below five safe paid places
Renew after 2031 only with insured room and five safe fees covering hire/cleaning/teaching/prep/travel
Keep booked orchestra calls and three paid pupils while testing flute circle

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my grown children that ten years until AGI by 2036 lets me ask what retirement will really pay. Flute-playing robots follow around 2039. A birthday will not cover the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I may still want and need paid music. Four months saved helps, but I cannot promise to stop without seeing pension figures and our regular bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would request my actual pension estimate and save fifteen percent of every extra paid concert after rent, food and flute repairs until we reach six months of expenses. In the first year after 2036 I would keep orchestra and pupils while booked; if live calls fall, I would seek a posted school tutor job only if my degree and teaching qualify, written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and the bus works. I would leave only after a signed suitable offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel uneasy about the distant mix of work and retirement, with current calls and a four-month reserve. Ten years give me time to check facts rather than declare a date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there are no extra concerts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then there is no fifteen percent to save from that source. I would not take it from food or rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop playing when robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would look at actual paid calls and the pension estimate. I will not leave pupils who pay me because a calendar says I am old enough.

say: I would ask what **retirement really pays** before planning to stop.
I would separate **2036 thinking AGI** from 2039 flute-playing robots.
think: At **68**, I may still need paid playing and teaching.
Our **four-month reserve** does not prove retirement affordable.
do: Request **actual pension estimate** and save 15% of extra paid concerts after rent/food/repairs toward six months.
Keep **orchestra and pupils** after 2036 while booked until a suitable signed offer.
Seek **posted tutor work** after live cuts only if degree/teaching qualify, written net after travel replaces losses and bus fits.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about distant work with current paid calls and savings.
S4.quote: A birthday will not cover the rent.
fieldNote: Her **six-month goal** comes from fifteen percent of truly extra paid concerts after essentials.
The **retirement choice** depends on actual pension figures and paid calls, not an assumed entitlement.

steps.text: Request actual pension estimate; keep paid orchestra/pupils after 2036 while booked
Save 15% of extra paid concerts after rent/food/repairs toward six months
Seek posted tutor job after live cuts if music degree/teaching qualify and bus fits
Require written net after travel replacing losses; keep music until signed offer

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the warm-up fees could stop before I know whether live calls hold. Signed orchestra dates, an actual pension estimate and a posted tutor role with written net pay after travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays for the journey to teach five flute beginners. A full room can still leave me unpaid if the fee sheet forgets my bus fare.

headlineQuote: A full room can still leave me unpaid if the fee sheet forgets my bus fare.
portrait: At **58**, Freya is an experienced flautist with a music degree, partner, grown children and four months saved.
Her **typical pay** comes from orchestra calls, warm-up recordings and three pupils, with some local jobs.
She has **never used AI** and checks notices on a paper calendar.
She tests a **paid beginner circle** only with written room terms and five fees covering full teaching costs and safe instruments.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end a quarter of Freya’s income from warm-up recordings.
whatWouldHelp: **Signed orchestra dates**, an actual pension estimate and qualifying posted tutor work with written after-travel replacement pay would help.
